national.title: Baby found "clinging to life" after being buried in crate for 24 hours
national.summary: An infant was found alive after apparently being buried in a dog crate for about 24 hours, authorities in South Carolina said.
national.body: A baby was found alive in South Carolina, after apparently being buried in a dog crate for about 24 hours, authorities said Tuesday.Eleven-month-old Koah Sharp had been missing since Monday, when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer traveled to multiple locations around Lexington County, the sheriff said, citing investigators. He was arrested on a burglary charge by county deputies on Monday night, but his son wasn't with him at the time.Sharp was located inside the crate, which was wrapped in a towel, about 50 yards from the home belonging to his grandfather, who is also Comer's father, Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. Search parties, involving almost 100 law enforcement and public safety officers, had been scouring the area for the infant since he went missing. One group spotted what Koon described as a patch of "freshly disturbed dirt" in a wooded area, Koon said.As officers started digging, they could hear Sharp cry, said Koon."So, as you imagine, the race was on. Everybody's getting down there, trying to get him out," the sheriff said.The officers discovered Sharp "clinging to life," according to Koon, who called the infant's cries "the most joyful sound you ever heard of a crying baby."The infant was immediately taken to a hospital for medical treatment.Koon said that Sharp had been in the care of his grandmother, Patricia Comer, on Monday. Michael Comer stayed with the baby at her house while she went out to run an errand, and, by the time a scheduled caregiver arrived shortly after, Comer was gone with his son. CBS affiliate WLTX reported that, when Patricia Comer learned the infant had been found, she jumped out of her car and shouted, "He's alive!"The investigation into what happened to Sharp was still in its early stages when Koon spoke at Tuesday's conference, and the sheriff said his department was working with the solicitor's office to determine which charges, if any, would be filed in the case.

national.title: Iran vows not to give up "a single particle" of nuclear material
national.summary: President Trump has repeatedly cited Iran's nuclear program as the core reason for going to war, but Tehran says it will not hand over any of its enriched uranium.
national.body: President Trump said Wednesday the U.S. has already won the war against Iran, but when the conflict will end is a different question. "America did not start a war with Iran," he said at a Veterans Day event at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. "Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. This should have been taken care of a long time ago." "Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back," he continued. "All of us fought back. We fought back. And we seriously fought back. And we won. Just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory. It's going to be total. It'll take them 25 years to rebuild back what we have destroyed, and hopefully we won't have to destroy any more of that country." The president reminded Americans that the Korean War lasted much longer and cost more lives, as did the Vietnam War and the Iraq War. As he has been saying for months, Mr. Trump said the conflict will be over soon.

national.title: Veterans groups keep focus on traumatic brain injuries
national.summary: Dozens of service members have suffered TBIs during the current conflict with Iran, and hundreds of thousands of veterans have been diagnosed during the Global War on Terrorism.
national.body: This Veterans Day, advocates are raising awareness about traumatic brain injury and the impact of these types of wounds on the post-9/11 military generation. Dozens of service members have suffered TBIs during the current conflict with Iran, and hundreds of thousands of veterans have been diagnosed with it over the quarter-century of the U.S.'s global war on terrorism. The recovery can be lifelong."The only thing I sort of remember is kind of a mayday call," Army veteran Jon Kohl told CBS News, recalling his 2013 helicopter crash in Afghanistan.The crash happened just one month shy of Kohl's 25th birthday, leaving him gravely wounded, including with a severe TBI."The first moment I saw him, I said it was a miracle he was alive," said his mother, Micha Kohl.His parents rushed to the military hospital in Landstuhl, Germany, to be by their son's side."They had to remove about a quarter to a third of his skull to relieve the pressure," said Paul Kohl.It would be a year before Jon Kohl could swallow, and doctors said there was a good chance he wouldn't be able to walk or talk ever again. However, he proved them wrong.Thirteen years later, regular art and music therapy are aiding Jon Kohl's recovery."One of the oddities of his brain injury is that, while he doesn't remember people talking or things he's reading, he remembers all the music he knew beforehand," his father said.The special therapeutic services are provided through the Wounded Warrior Project's Independence Program, which aids veterans with moderate to severe brain injuries, spinal cord injuries or neurological conditions. national.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
national.summary: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
national.body:
Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.

Demonstrations have taken place across the country, including in Madrid and Barcelona, where tens of thousands marched in the evening.

Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.

The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."

However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.

Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.

The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.

The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

national.summary: A new bill would bring scrutiny to pardons tied to the president's allies and donors, but legal experts say it would likely run up against the Constitution.
national.body: House Democrats who lead the "End Corruption Caucus" have introduced legislation seeking to rein in what has been called the "pardon economy" that has flourished during President Trump's second term, according to lawmakers and a copy of the bill.On Wednesday, Reps. Mike Levin and Jason Crow unveiled the Abuse of the Pardon Prevention Act — a measure aimed at acts of clemency that raise possible conflicts of interest or could involve favors for the president's allies and donors. America has "a pardon industrial complex" where "you literally, for the highest dollar amount, can go and buy a pardon," Levin said in an exclusive interview with CBS News this week. "That is not how the Founders intended for this to work," said Levin, a California Democrat. "The pardon power is intended to be used in cases of justice and mercy."The bill stands almost no chance of surviving Mr. Trump's veto pen, yet it offers an early look at how Democrats, fresh off sweeping midterm wins, may use their new majorities to scrutinize Mr. Trump's freewheeling use of the pardon power. national.title: Stacy Keach, star of "Mike Hammer" TV series and stage, dies at 85
national.summary: Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV, has died. He was 85.
national.body: Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. He was 85. Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure," his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017. Though he was considered a preeminent interpreter of Shakespeare and a favorite of such legendary directors as John Huston, Keach was indelibly linked with his take on the hard-boiled Hammer, the fictitious TV private detective created by crime novelist Mickey Spillane.Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating "World's Most Amazing Videos" on TV. He played a deranged colonel in "The Ninth Configuration" (also known as "Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane"), led the TV show "Titus," had a role in Alexander Payne's Oscar-nominated drama "Nebraska," and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama "Blue Bloods." Last year, he had an excellent turn as George Clooney's bitter father in "Jay Kelly." "My objective was to have as varied a selection of roles as possible. It probably did hurt my career," he told New York magazine in 2012. "My choices have had a cost attached to it. One of the greats. Proud to have shared some frames with him." national.title: Mississippi Senate race leans Democratic as Colom's lead grows
national.summary: The Senate race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, as Democrat Scott Colom has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
national.body: Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi leans toward Democrat Scott Colom, who has mounted a surprisingly competitive challenge against incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. As of midday Wednesday, Colom was leading Hyde-Smith by over 3,100 votes, with 98% of the vote in, according to CBS News projections. At one point on the morning after the election, a mere few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State. The state's top election official, Secretary of State Michael Watson, said in a post on X Monday that seven more counties of the state's 82 counties still needed to upload their unofficial results, with certified results due from all the counties by Friday. He also said 2,732 absentee mail ballots were still out, and the deadline for election officials to receive them would be Tuesday, Nov. 10. Hyde-Smith, asked by CBS News' Caitlin Huey-Burns what she could have done differently during the campaign to make it less competitive, responded, "I think we worked very hard and had a very good campaign."Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge in a state President Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Mississippi hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982. Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races in the midterms, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. Democrats have secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority. Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost-of-living and healthcare issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.Speaking to supporters in the wee hours after election night, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction.""We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson said Friday there are approximately 3,300 outstanding mail ballots. national.title: Greetings from Senegal, where breakdancers are competing in the Youth Olympics
national.summary: Senegal's breakdancers have been practicing for their country's historic hosting of the Youth Olympic Games this month. It's the first time Africa is hosting an Olympic event.
national.body:
Ricci Shrylock/NPR Hip-hop music blasted over a portable speaker while half-a-dozen teenagers practiced their best breakdancing moves in Senagal's capital Dakar. They glided on their shins and jumped into the air, clutched their heels and struck midair poses.

Senegal's breakdancers were honing their craft ahead of the country's historic hosting of the Youth Olympic Games this month. It's the first time an Olympic event is being held on African soil.

I took the photo above last month as 15-year-old Suzanne Toure struck a breakdancing pose. She is the only girl on the Senegal National Sport Dance and Break Team. Three years ago, her little brother introduced her to breakdancing.

Dancers on the Senegalese team mix traditional moves into their routines from national styles such as mbalax and Yela , swirling their arms and legs in a windmill-like motion. "You can sense some American and European influence in our routines, yes, but there are also African dances. It's about mixing these African dances into the breaking," says coach Francis Siméon Gomis.

They see this as their chance to show the world what their nation can offer on the dance floor, and hope to win a medal on home turf.

national.summary: White House counsel Will Scharf warned that congressional subpoenas could lead to investigations from the executive branch.
national.body: Washington — The top lawyer in the White House warned the leading Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee that investigations into the Trump administration that lawmakers plan to pursue in the next Congress "may cross the line into blatant criminality" and said congressional subpoenas could prompt probes from the executive branch.The message from White House counsel Will Scharf to Rep. national.body: The Black college students who were harassed by two White students at the University of Mississippi making monkey gestures and sounds outside their apartment are speaking out after the incident went viral.The women said they were familiar with the stories of racism some faced at Ole Miss over the years — the school didn't allow its first Black student, James Meredith, until 1962, for instance — but they were not prepared for what they experienced last Friday.Jakirya Metcalf, a freshman at Ole Miss, said she was in her apartment last Friday night when she saw the video on her Ring camera."We actually went outside and tried to, like, approach them and get them to explain why they did that," Metcalf told "CBS Mornings.""One girl was like, 'I'm sorry we did that to four doors,'" Victoria Johnson, one of the roommates, said. national.summary: Microsoft outlines the pledges it makes to data center communities as industry tries to sway public opinion on AI.

Microsoft president Brad Smith told CBS News about the pledge it makes to the communities where it builds and operates data centers. "Basically, we will put the community first," he said. "We will not do anything that will increase the electricity rates of our neighbors. national.title: Kennedy relatives join the fight against Trump's arch, alleging harm to JFK's grave
national.summary: Nine members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal fight against Trump's D.C. arch, arguing it would disrupt views and cast shadows over their ancestors' graves at Arlington National Cemetery.
national.body:
One of America's most prominent political dynasties has waded into the growing fight against President Trump's proposed arch in Washington, D.C.

Nine members of the Kennedy family filed suit in federal court on Tuesday to block the 250-foot structure, saying it would obstruct their relatives' gravesites — including the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame — at nearby Arlington National Cemetery.

"A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on behalf of the family.

Politics A judge blocked construction of Trump's arch at the 11th hour. What's next? The plaintiffs include children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy and a son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy, all three of whom are buried at Arlington National Cemetery. There is one noticeable absence: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., did not join his siblings in the lawsuit against his own administration.

"It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told NPR in a statement. "We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds."

The Kennedys' motion, filed hours before Veterans' Day, adds a highly personal layer to the ongoing legal fight.

"[The arch] constitutes nothing less than a permanent denigration of the Kennedy Gravesites and the final resting place for Plaintiffs' parents and grandparents," they wrote in their 27-page filing . "Plaintiffs would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended."

The Kennedys seek to join the existing federal lawsuit against the arch, which combines two cases: one brought by Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian earlier this year, and another filed by the governments of D.C. and Virginia late last month. The Arlington County Board has also filed a lawsuit in Virginia.

national.title: Three Iran-backed suspects plotted attacks including incident near UK air base, US says
national.summary: The US Department of Justice says the men were involved in a string of plots, including a major incident near RAF Fairford, which is used by US armed forces.
national.body:
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has announced charges against three Iran-backed operatives that it alleges were involved in a string of plots in the US and Europe.

The DOJ said Iranian agents most recently "orchestrated a terrorist plot at an air force base in the United Kingdom", saying they were involved in the major incident in September near RAF Fairford in the UK, where US armed forces were stationed.

The three men have been accused by the DOJ of being involved in 18 attacks and attempted attacks, including in London, Amsterdam and Paris. Some of the incidents were said to be directed by the men over FaceTime.

The DOJ said they acted in the name of the group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI).

Iranian Mohsen Mohajeri, Iraqi national Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and dual Iranian-Iraqi citizen Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi were charged in an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the DOJ said.

The DOJ said that most recently, al-Hassani "orchestrated a terrorist plot" at RAF Fairford - where on 27 September a major incident was declared after suspicious vans were reported near the base.

national.title: Bessent relocates from home to military base after Iran threats
national.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a U.S. military base.
national.body: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life."The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said. The decision comes as Bessent has spearheaded a U.S. push to cripple Iran's economy, vowing an "economic onslaught" against Tehran through a web of sanctions. The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation. A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move. "After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News. CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment.U.S. national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned last month that Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.Those efforts include beefing up the targeting of current and former U.S. officials such as Bessent, the Times reported. Iranian plotting against U.S. officials has reached a "more advanced stage," according to the anonymous sources cited in the Times. Clayton's warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, came as the State Department adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pared back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen. The U.S. military has also removed some aircraft from two British bases in recent weeks following reported threats from Iran. Diplomatic efforts to end the war are gathering steam, with Rubio saying on Tuesday that he saw no need to resume major combat operations against Iran because economic sanctions and other restrictions were working so effectively.

Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.

national.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
national.summary: The news comes at a turbulent time for Prabowo, who faces a growing rift with his predecessor Joko Widodo.
national.body:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.

It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.

The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.

The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.

"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.

national.title: Hoax bomb threats affect at least 20 European flights within hours
national.summary: At least 20 flights in Europe deal with bomb threats, adding to what one expert calls an unusual level of hoaxes in a short time period, suggesting "a very deliberate act."
national.body: Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act." British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent. The business consequences alone of not doing so, even if the threat is proven to be a hoax, would be prohibitive – and you can imagine the cost if it turned out to be genuine."The flights impacted on Thursday included:A flight from Ireland to Italy that was diverted to an air base in western France Thursday because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office. national.title: Biden targeted by protesters after event in Ireland
national.summary: Protesters targeted former President Joe Biden and members of his family as they exited an event in Dublin, Ireland, on Tuesday night.
national.body: Washington — Protesters targeted former President Joe Biden and members of his family as they exited an event in Dublin, Ireland, on Tuesday night, leading to several arrests.Biden, former first lady Jill Biden and son Hunter Biden were at Trinity College, where Hunter Biden was being honored with a gold medal by the College Historical Society. The protests outside escalated as the Bidens were leaving, according to university spokesperson Catherine O'Mahony. According to the University Times, the protesters chanted "shame on you" and "Genocide Joe" at the Bidens. Photos showed protesters waving a Palestinian flag. O'Mahony said the Bidens left without incident. Irish police An Garda Síochána confirmed that three people were arrested Tuesday night in connection with the protests, and a man in his 50s has been charged. The other two men, one in his 30s and another a late teen, were released, police said.The event coincided with publicity around Biden's new memoir, "Promise Me, America," which is set to be published next week. On Wednesday morning, People published an on-camera interview with the former president, his first since leaving the White House.Biden was diagnosed with Stage 4 prostate cancer shortly after leaving office, and it has spread to his bones. He told People that he would not have run for reelection had he been diagnosed while president."I would've not gone forward, because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for [president]," Biden said. "But that wasn't the case ... I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job." Biden writes in his book that it's a "cynical twist" that many Americans believe he hid his cancer diagnosis, when he says he was not diagnosed until May 2025."We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on," Biden told People. "I think it's important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through ... I wasn't hiding it at all." Hunter Biden told CBS News partner BBC News earlier this year that his father's cancer has "spread, metastasized into his bones and further," adding "it's very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects."

Peltola's campaign also said it wants to know the reasons for the rejections and said its intent is to ensure that all qualified voters have their ballots counted. Attorneys for the state say the information requested would violate voter privacy.

national.summary: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's powerful AI computer chips, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
national.body: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported. And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall. Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China. President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related). Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter, and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship. national.title: Enrolling in Medicare? Here's what to consider before Dec. 7.
national.summary: Medicare open enrollment, which runs from Oct.15 to Dec. 7, gives people a chance to change their health coverage. Here's what to know.
national.body: The Medicare open enrollment window has arrived, giving millions of seniors across the U.S. the chance to revisit their coverage choices. Even if you're happy with your plan, experts say it's still worth exploring your options.Health plans change every year, meaning people could see updates to premium costs, prescription drug coverage and available providers in their network. New plans also come online, expanding the already broad list of coverage options."There's really no one who can't benefit from at least taking some time to take a look," Alex Cottrill, senior policy analyst with KFF's program on Medicare policy, told CBS News.People enrolled in Medicare Advantage or a Part D prescription drug plan typically receive an "Annual Notice of Change" in September outlining any updates to their coverage, according to Medicare.gov, the government website for the program."Pay attention to those notices, and frankly, even if you don't receive an annual notice of change, you still want to review your current plan and make sure that it is the right one for you," said Jessica Rivkin, vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors, an insurance agency that helps people enroll in Medicare Advantage plans.Americans now have less than a month to make their Medicare choices, with open enrollment set to close Dec. 7. national.title: At least 3 killed when SUV crashes into North Hollywood food stand
national.summary: At least three people were killed and two others were severely injured when an SUV crashed into a food stand near a Metro bus stop in North Hollywood.
national.body: Police say three people are dead after an SUV crashed into a food stand near a North Hollywood bus stop in Los Angeles on Tuesday night. The collision occurred at around 5:55 p.m. local time near the Metro station at the corner of Lankershim and Chandler boulevards, according to the LA Police Department. Firefighters said three people were pronounced dead at the scene, while three others were taken to a nearby hospital, two of whom were in critical condition at the time. As of 11 p.m., one of the victims remained in stable condition, while the other was still critical.The LAPD said the victims were each Latina women between the ages of 40 and 60. They're yet to be identified publicly, pending notification of next of kin.The critically injured individuals are also Latina women between 50 and 55 years old.Crews extricated one person, the driver, from the wreckage, according to LAFD."I'm heartbroken for the families of everyone impacted," Mayor Karen Bass wrote in a statement on X. "We will continue to provide updates as more information becomes available."LAPD officers said the driver of the white SUV was in serious condition and was determined to be under the influence of drugs or alcohol at the time of the crash.The driver was identified by police as Ihor Demianenko, a Valley Village resident. He was arrested on suspicion of three counts of murder.He's currently being held on more than $6 million bail.The circumstances surrounding the collision remain under investigation, but LAPD Major Collision Investigation Team and Valley Traffic Division detectives said that Demianenko was attempting to avoid another car that was driving "legally and safely" before the crash. Police said they would continue looking for security camera footage from the Metro bus station and businesses in the surrounding area as their probe continued."It'll be a prolonged but a very deliberate investigation to determine what happened here," LAPD Chief Jim McDonnell said. "Our hearts go out to the families of the victims that were struck here tonight."Aerial footage showed the white SUV stopped on the sidewalk underneath a canopy, where the food stand was set up. Witnesses told CBS LA the three deceased victims were street vendors in the area, one of whom worked there for more than 15 years.This is a developing story. Check back for details.

Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty asked a judge Tuesday to block President Donald Trump's plan to build a towering memorial arch, saying the 250-foot structure would cast a shadow over their relatives' gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery.

President Donald Trump is expected to lay a wreath at Arlington National Cemetery at 11 a.m. EST before making remarks for Veterans Day. Watch live in the video player above.

The shadow would "fundamentally alter the experience of visiting the gravesites," the relatives argued. They filed a motion to intervene in two existing lawsuits seeking to block construction of the arch.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan last week prohibited the Trump administration from breaking ground on the structure for 14 days.

Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News

The nine Kennedy family members who filed suit are children and grandchildren of Robert F. Kennedy and Edward M. Kennedy, brothers of the slain U.S. president John F. Kennedy, both of whom served in the U.S. Senate. They are buried close to the eternal flame that marks JFK's gravesite, a trio of memorials that are a major draw for the millions of people who visit the Arlington cemetery each year.

Building the arch would be a "permanent denigration" of the gravesites, and the Kennedy offspring "would never again be able to appreciate both sites as they always have before, and as the Kennedy family always intended," lawyers for the relatives wrote. national.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
national.summary: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
national.body:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.

Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.

Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.

Both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.

This latest round of talks had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.

For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.

national.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
national.summary: Leonardo Bertulazzi, a former member of the Marxist guerrilla group the Red Brigades, was about to be extradited to his home country of Italy.
national.body:
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.

Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.

His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.

Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.

He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.

Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.

When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.

Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.

national.title: Following big Democratic wins, these swing voters are looking for results
national.summary: For the swing voters NPR is regularly checking in with as part of its Swing Shift series, the election results brought mixed emotions, as does the pending Democratic control of Congress.
national.body:
Swing voters Theresa from Pennsylvania, Jason from North Carolina and Gerald from Georgia. All three voted in this year's midterms and all three have mixed emotions about the results. Tara Anand for NPR hide caption

Republicans were dealt a stunning rebuke in last week's midterms. But swing voters, who could be decisive in the next election, are more interested in results than investigations or impeachment as Democrats prepare to take power in Congress.

"I am hoping that we don't experience a bunch of gridlock and a lot of whining and crying and just political infighting for the next two years," said Theresa, a voter from Pennsylvania who is participating in NPR's Swing Shift project. "I'm hoping we don't have that. I fear that we will have that."

NPR has agreed not to use the full names of the Swing Shift voters, so they can speak freely about politics without fear of personal or professional repercussions.

Theresa voted for President Biden in 2020, President Trump in 2024 and split her ticket in this year's midterms. Like many voters, her top issue this year was affordability. In a voice memo sent to NPR days after the midterms, Theresa said she is eager for the cost of living to come down.

"I just don't remember it ever being as bad in our time," Theresa said. "And I'm just hoping we get some relief and we get some relief soon."

At 9:56 PM on election night, Wally in Georgia hit send on his voice memo. He had seen enough.

"Just checking in here with a quick note. I'm not surprised at all by the outcome tonight," Wally said. "I believe that this is a lot of Trump's doing and pushback on his style of politics and how he governs."

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, both sides said Wednesday as two days of U.S. mediated talks concluded with no major breakthrough on ending Moscow's nearly 5-year-old full-scale invasion.

Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement.

national.title: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
national.summary: Mada Masr editor-in-chief Lina Attalah is being tried on the charge of "publishing false news" and potentially faces imprisonment.
national.body:
A criminal court in Cairo has postponed the retrial of the prominent Egyptian journalist Lina Attalah, whose case has drawn international condemnation.

Wednesday's opening hearing was adjourned until 18 November after defence lawyers representing the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr requested a new judge.

The UN has warned of "widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists".

Attalah told the BBC that a recent crackdown was meant to "send a chilling message" to "the very few newsrooms that are left".

She warned: "Everybody should be careful, everybody should be scared, everybody should be wondering if they are next."

Set up 13 years ago, Mada Masr became Egypt's leading independent news site with Attalah as its editor-in-chief and co-founder.

Last month, the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court convicted her of running a website without a licence - which she said she had tried in vain for years to obtain. She was issued a hefty fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds ($56,000; £42,000) and Mada Masr was ordered to shut down.

After that trial, Attalah found that a court had previously given her a one-year prison sentence, without her knowledge, for "spreading false news" - a charge often used against journalists and dissidents - as well as operating a website without a licence. It was issued in absentia in 2024, even though she was in the country at the time. Attalah is now being retried in that case by the same judge.

national.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
national.summary: The sow and her three cubs were responsible for killing Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.
national.body:
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.

Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.

The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.

All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.

Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada

Published 6 days ago "Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.

The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".

He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".

national.title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status
national.summary: The country begins a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free, provided no new cases are recorded.
national.body:
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.

It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.

He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.

Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.

"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.

"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.

national.title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
national.summary: More than 6,000 Italian schools received a threat. Authorities in all three countries say there appears to be no risk to the public. It is not known if the incidents are linked.
national.body:
Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.

In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".

"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.

Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.

"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.

Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.

"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.

Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.

national.summary: The 400 Mawozo gang was targeted by El Salvador's military, which has deployed thousands of troops to combat Haiti's gang violence crisis.
national.body:
Haiti's Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé has praised "the commitment of the Salvadorean forces in the fight against gangs" after a joint strike on a house allegedly used by the leader of the 400 Mawozo gang.

El Salvador's President, Nayib Bukele, had earlier announced that a joint task force had "destroyed" what he described as "the house of Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters".

A small contingent of Salvadorean troops has been in Haiti since January 2025 as part of a multinational force deployed to suppress gang violence.

Last month, Bukele sent an extra 2,000 soldiers to rescue four Salvadoreans who have been missing since they were ambushed on 18 October.

Bukele's post on X , external was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex.

As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

Writing in Creole, Bukele said "we kept our promise", adding that the alleged gang members "ran away without even trying to fight".

Local media reported that as many as 20 people were killed in the strike, which they said was carried out in the early hours of Sunday.

national.title: US House blocks bid to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth
national.summary: Trump welcomes the outcome, praising Hegseth as a "Great American Patriot", but Democrats can try again next year.
national.body:
An effort to impeach US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war on Iran without congressional authorisation, has failed on Capitol Hill.

A majority of the House of Representatives voted to refer impeachment articles to a committee - essentially killing the effort introduced by dissident Republican congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky.

During an earlier briefing, Hegseth called the impeachment effort a "farce" and "sabotage".

The bid to find the cabinet secretary guilty of misconduct and ultimately remove him from office was seen as a long shot as it could have required a number of other Republicans to defy President Donald Trump.

That calculation might change in January, when the opposition Democratic Party assumes control of both chambers of Congress, following its successes in the US midterm elections. For now, Trump's Republican Party remains in control.

After Tuesday's vote, the most senior Democrat in the House, Hakeem Jeffries, said: "This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning."

The question on which lawmakers were voting on Tuesday was whether or not to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, which is led by Republicans. The alternative would have been to allow the resolution to proceed in the House itself.

All Republicans other than Massie voted to refer the resolution to the committee, meaning that the congressman's effort failed in a 211-204 vote.

national.title: Transport workers in Chile block highways in protest over surging fuel prices
national.summary: Hundreds of bus and lorry drivers are blocking traffic along major highway routes across the country.
national.body:
Hundreds of transport workers in Chile have blocked roads and highways across the country in protest over high fuel prices.

Drivers of busses and lorries began protesting on Tuesday, gathering in convoys to halt traffic along major routes.

They are demanding a relief from surging diesel prices, which have been driven up by the war in Iran.

Talks between government officials and protest leaders have so far failed to reach a resolution, with another meeting expected to take place on Wednesday.

The protest is being organised by the ⁠Fuerza del Norte trade union, which represents around 80% of Chile's lorry drivers, and the No+TAG civic protest ​movement.

"There is no point of agreement with the government that could offer any perspective to find solutions for everyone," Andrés Alarcón, a spokesman for No+TAG, said after talks broke down on Tuesday, adding "the strike continues".

Economy Minister Daniel Mas called for further dialogue, but warned "at some point, we will have to clear the highways".

He stressed the protests were impacting economic activity and exports, saying "we need to get the country moving again".

local.body:
A Flock Safety camera outside Fredonia Village Hall was shut off and its removal was requested, according to Fredonia Trustee Ben Brauchler.

Brauchler devoted his report at Monday's Fredonia Board of Trustees meeting to some news that should hearten the many opponents of the Flock program.

"As I understand it, the (Chautauqua County) district attorney (Jason Schmidt) has requested that Flock remove the camera in front of Village Hall," Brauchler said. "That request is pending. The camera is still there, but it is currently apparently disconnected."

That camera, looming above the corner of Church and Temple streets, has irritated numerous residents. They cite concerns about privacy and improper data sharing. One resident, Patrick Sexton, went so far as to declare he does not drive through that intersection since the Flock camera was placed there.

Brauchler continued, "There are two other cameras in this immediate vicinity but they're not on village property and (Schmidt) tells us we don't have any jurisdiction over them. Perhaps the town of Pomfret (board), when they address this Wednesday night, will be able to do something about it, with any luck."

Schmidt's District Attorney's Office contracted with Flock Safety about a year ago to install the cameras around the county as a crime-fighter. The DA defended the program in comments to the OBSERVER last week, and also did so at a September Fredonia trustees meeting.

OBSERVER Photos by Braden Carmen Fredonia Central School students are pictured with local military veterans at the conclusion of a Veterans Day assembly on Tuesday morning.

Pictured is Fredonia’s version of a “Missing Man Table”, which honors fallen, missing in action, or prisoner of war service members.

Roughly two dozen veterans attended an assembly at the Fredonia Central School auditorium on Tuesday morning.

Veterans gave high fives as they were greeted by second-grade students and presented with gifts on Tuesday.

Fredonia students filled the auditorium on Tuesday morning for a meaningful assembly that reminded everyone of the purpose of the day that followed.

The annual Veterans Day celebration at Fredonia Central Schools had even more meaning this year than ever before. Students in Cathy Cruver's leadership course led the way this year, organizing an assembly to honor roughly two dozen distinguished guests.

The assembly lasted roughly 30 minutes, with students leading each portion of the event. Mikaela Sciarrino sang the national anthem, then each branch of the military was recognized. Members in attendance stood to a round of applause.

One of the many guests at Tuesday's event was Dewey Winchell, a World War II veteran of the U.S. Navy. Winchell is 101 years old. He served in the Navy from 1943-1946 shortly after graduating from Fredonia High School.

local.title: Rochester launches effort to help homeowners go solar
local.summary: The initiative will bring homeowners together to leverage their collective purchasing power and negotiate competitive pricing from qualified local installers, according to a city news release.
local.body:
A new effort by the city of Rochester aims to help residents afford solar energy and save on electricity costs.

The city is partnering with the global provider Switch Together, which will act as a group buyer for residential solar installations. The initiative will bring homeowners together to leverage their collective purchasing power and negotiate competitive pricing from qualified local installers, according to a city news release. There's a Dec. 16 deadline to register and accept an offer.

Through the program, homeowners will be able to review a personalized solar installation offer and decide whether to move forward. Homeowners can register on Switch Together's website, where they can also find out more information about the program and their property's suitability for solar.

The city and its partner are also holding a virtual Solar 101 information session for residents from 6 to 7 p.m. on Nov. 19. Registration is required and can be completed on Switch Together's site.

The city receives no compensation through the program but also incurs no cost, according to the release.

local.summary: Just ahead of Veterans Day, Erie County is taking steps to provide financial relief to seriously disabled veterans through a new property tax exemption.
local.body: Just ahead of Veterans Day, Erie County is taking steps to provide financial relief to seriously disabled veterans through a new property tax exemption.County Executive Mark Poloncarz signed a local law allowing qualifying veterans with a 100% service-connected disability to receive a full exemption from the Erie County portion of property taxes on their primary residence.The law allows Erie County to opt in to a benefit authorized under New York state law.“It gave municipalities the ability to opt in to a provision that would then exempt any individual who has been determined to be 100% disabled as a result of their service in one of the military branches in our country,” Poloncarz said.Poloncarz said the exemption is a way to recognize the sacrifices made by veterans who have been permanently disabled because of their military service.“This is a way of thanking our men and women who unfortunately, due to their service, are permanently disabled,” he said.Erie County Legislator Lindsay Lorigo, who represents West Seneca, said the county has the ability to provide the tax relief to eligible veterans.“It was a really simple thing to do, and we know that we can afford to offer veterans that are 100% disabled status a total exemption from Erie County,” Lorigo said. “So I am really proud to be here, and I am really proud of the county executive for signing this into law.”For qualifying veterans who own and occupy their primary residence, the exemption means they will no longer have to pay the Erie County portion of their property taxes.“With regard to their primary residence as a homeowner, they will not have to pay taxes to Erie County going forward,” Poloncarz said.WATCH: Erie County approves property tax exemption for seriously disabled veteransVeterans will need to apply to receive the benefit. local.title: NY lawmakers weigh new restrictions on license plate reader cameras amid concerns over surveillance and abuse
local.summary: State lawmakers are considering new restrictions on automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology amid concerns about how the information is collected, stored and shared.
local.body: State lawmakers are considering new restrictions on automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology amid concerns about how the information is collected, stored and shared.The issue was the focus of an Assembly hearing that brought together law enforcement officials, civil liberties advocates and other experts. The debate grew tense at times, with lawmakers challenging claims that the technology is not a threat to constitutional privacy rights.The cameras, often associated with the Flock brand, photograph passing vehicles and capture license plate information, along with the time and location of each scan. The information can then be stored and searched by law enforcement.Assemblymember Nily Rozic, who chairs the Assembly's Consumer Affairs and Protection Committee, said New York lacks consistent statewide rules governing the technology."In New York, we currently lack universal minimum standards governing the collection, retention, and use sharing of information through these systems," Rozic said. "We probably should not leave the protection of New Yorkers' information entirely to the discretion of individual agencies or private companies."Tyler Nims, chief of the state Attorney General's Law Enforcement Misconduct Investigative Office, said the cameras collect information about millions of innocent drivers."Every day in New York, ALPRs capture and store data regarding the movement of millions of people who are not violating any laws," Nims testified.Nims said that information can be shared among local and federal agencies, raising concerns about how it could be used to track immigrants, protesters and people seeking reproductive or gender-affirming health care.He also acknowledged a major challenge for people concerned about the technology: they may never know their information has been accessed.Asked how an innocent New Yorker would discover they had been tracked, Nims said, "I think the answer is there's no way, unless there was some, you know, unless there's some kind of action taken as a result of that, they would never know."Law enforcement officials who testified argued that license plate readers are an important investigative tool that can help police solve crimes and protect the public.Raymond Tierney, the Suffolk County district attorney, called ALPRs "a critical tool in investigating, solving, and preventing crime."He described a case from Decemb

local.summary: Buffalo's 23-6 win over the Minnesota Vikings moved the Bills to 7-1 and ended that 33-year wait. For Bills fans, the milestone is also an opportunity to think about just how much life has changed since 1993.
local.body: A lot has changed since the last time the Buffalo Bills started a season 7-1.It was 1993. Most people didn't carry a cell phone, streaming wasn't a thing, and Blockbuster was a popular place to rent a movie on VHS.Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" dominated the music charts, the national average for a gallon of regular gasoline was around $1.17, and a dozen chicken wings could cost you around $4.It was a different time, but a familiar start for the Bills.On Nov. 7, 1993, Buffalo improved to 7-1 with a 13-10 overtime victory over the New England Patriots."A Buffalo offense that sputtered all day long finally made two big passing plays when it had to, and in the end it was Steve Christie that made the biggest play of them all," then-Eyewitness Sports reporter John Murphy said from New England. "So the Bills make the turn at 7-1 on the year," added Sports Anchor Jerry Azar from the studio. "I was actually stationed at Camp David, the presidential retreat."For Amanda Alford, of Buffalo, 1993 is a little harder to remember."I was 1 year old," Alford said. "I was born in 1992, so yeah, I wasn't sure what was happening."Bill Willcox, of Lancaster, remembers being at a very different point in his life."I had some young daughters, I was married, I lived in Hamburg," Willcox said.But Buffalo's 7-1 record is more than a trip down memory lane. local.summary: The Buffalo Common Council has approved nearly $35 million in emergency borrowing to pay for repairs and other capital needs across the city, despite warnings from Comptroller Barbara Miller-Williams about taking on additional debt.
local.body: The Buffalo Common Council has approved nearly $35 million in emergency borrowing to pay for repairs and other capital needs across the city, despite warnings from Comptroller Barbara Miller-Williams about taking on additional debt.The resolution passed Tuesday afternoon with six members voting in favor, one voting against and two absent.Mayor Sean Ryan is seeking authorization for a total of $94 million in capital investment. local.title: 'Concerning': Buffalo councilmember presses for answers after police staffing problems revealed
local.summary: A 7 News investigation revealed Buffalo police overtime used to meet minimum staffing jumped 65% last fiscal year. Now a local lawmaker is demanding answers on the recruiting slump.
local.body: The city of Buffalo does not always have enough police officers to meet minimum staffing requirements, relying more and more on overtime to fill shifts. That's the result of a months-long investigation I revealed on Monday. Now, a local lawmaker has questions.Buffalo Common Councilmember David Rivera is chair of the council's Police Oversight Committee. He's reacting to the fact that police overtime used to cover minimum staffing requirements skyrocketed in 2025 to 2026 compared to the previous fiscal year. It was up 65%."It's alarming, it's concerning. You're dealing with public safety," Rivera said. "It's unfortunate that we haven't had a recruit class in the recent past."The last police exam was administered by the city in 2023. Speaking to me Monday, Police Commissioner Erika Shields put the problem down to the subsequent three-year pause, explaining that the Buffalo Police Department now aims to recruit through the next available state police exam in April 2027. WATCH: Buffalo councilmember presses for answers after police staffing revelationsRivera has asked the city's HR department to explain the reasons for the pause.One person who might know is Rivera's fellow councilmember, Christopher Scanlon. He was acting mayor from October 2024 through December 2025 at the time of that pause. He was unavailable to speak to me Tuesday.In the meantime, what about the council's role in all this? I asked Rivera whether this is something the council could have kept a closer eye on in the past."Well, we have a list, we have a current list that hasn't expired, that's still there until 2027," he said, referring to a list of people who have already passed the city's civil service police exam - the first step in becoming a police officer. "The question I have is why haven't we hired from that list?"I asked the mayor's office if that list is exhausted but have not yet heard anything back on that subject. An HR representative is expected to discuss the matter at the council meeting next Tuesday. local.summary: Britini D'Angelo, a special education teacher in Niagara Falls, was named by Kleenex as the National Hero of the Classroom. The award comes with cash prizes for both her and Kalfas Elementary.
local.body: Britini D'Angelo, a special education teacher in Niagara Falls, was named by Kleenex as the National Hero of the Classroom. The award comes with cash prizes for both her and Kalfas Elementary.For the past three years, Miss D'Angelo has brought smiles to students’ faces inside her Henry J. Kalfas Elementary School classroom.“I love my job more than I can express in words. This is what I am meant to do for the rest of my life,” D'Angelo said. Long before she ever decided on her professional career, her road to teaching started before her second birthday.“When I was 22 months old, I was diagnosed with autism. I was nonverbal, no eye contact, repetitive stims and no social cues,” D'Angelo said. “I had a one-to-one aide until the end of first grade, so I had a village fighting for my IEP every single day.”That village both taught her to be the person she is today and inspired her to pour into others in similar situations to what she had experienced growing up.“I want the absolute best for them every single day, and as their advocate, we are going to make sure that happens,” D'Angelo said.“She understands the kids a lot,” Najah Peterson, one of D'Angelo’s assistant teachers, said. “She always puts kids first, school first, and she’s so sweet. She’s willing to help everybody.”WATCH: ‘I love my job’: Niagara Falls teacher named National Hero of the Classroom by KleenexD’Angelo’s story has caught the attention of hundreds of thousands of followers online, 215,000 on Instagram and 679,000 on TikTok. Now, even the brand Kleenex is jumping on board, naming her their 2026 National Hero of the Classroom.The contest awarded D'Angelo $10,000 and a $5,000 donation to the school.“My cash prize for me, I’m putting in the bank, and I am saving,” D'Angelo said. “Most importantly, our school does win $5,000, which our school can absolutely use. I cannot wait to see what we spend the money on.”Beyond the money, the award comes with a year's supply of Kleenex tissues for the entire building.“I got like 15 boxes yesterday, and that is the first wave. I think we get them every month or two weeks or something. It’s crazy,” D'Angelo said.Join the Niagara County Community News Facebook group to connect with neighbors and learn about what's happening in your community.

local.body: Ten years ago, thick black smoke poured into the sky over Lackawanna when a massive fire ripped through the Steelworks Industrial Park off Route 5 — the site of the former Bethlehem Steel facility. I said, 'Get dressed and get out of here.' Well, it's too early. No, get out of here. We don't know what's over there... I packed the animals up and headed over to my son's house," said Murray.Great Lakes Industrial Development owned the building. A tenant — Industrial Materials Recycling — operated a plastics recycling center. The building also housed other businesses, including a storage facility, with a lot of materials that burned for 11 days.When I asked Murray what the worst part was for him, he pointed to the uncertainty."Anticipation of what might be over there. local.title: Gov. Hochul keeps the door open to redrawing New York’s congressional map
local.summary: The Democratic governor remains open to a constitutional amendment that would make it easier for her party to redraw the lines.
local.body:
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she remains open to a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for Democrats to redraw New York’s congressional districts as soon as 2028.

The Democratic governor told reporters Tuesday that major Democratic wins across the country in last week’s elections wouldn’t necessarily derail her party’s push to change the state constitution to allow for mid-decade redistricting in the Empire State.

But Hochul also didn’t commit to moving ahead with the plan, which was first put into motion last year as Republicans in Texas, North Carolina and other states began redrawing congressional districts to benefit their party.

The Republican efforts — backed by President Donald Trump — either backfired or didn’t matter, with Democrats easily picking up enough seats across the country to take control of the U.S. House of Representatives.

“Those newly drawn lines [in other states] are still there,” Hochul said at her Manhattan office. “And while it didn’t have an effect on this year’s election, there’s always another election every two years.”

The governor continued: “You can't assume that there's going to be the same outcomes every two years, and so I want to look at it long-term.”

In New York, the state constitution requires a bipartisan panel to redraw congressional lines after each once-a-decade Census, with lawmakers getting final approval. But it doesn’t provide a mechanism to change the districts during the intervening years.

In March, the U.S. Supreme Court halted a lower court’s order that would’ve required redrawing New York’s 11th congressional district , a Republican stronghold that includes all of Staten Island and parts of Brooklyn. The order was spurred by a Democrat-led lawsuit that argued the current district disenfranchised Black and Hispanic voters. Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, a Republican who has held the district since 2021, was re-elected last Tuesday.

local.title: Bello proposes 2027 budget that cuts the tax rate and funds a child care initiative
local.summary: But Monroe County Executive Adam Bello warned that the county is facing rising costs in several areas, combined with reduced or stagnant reimbursement rates from the state and federal government.
local.body:
Monroe County Executive Adam Bello's proposed 2027 budget would again cut the tax rate for property owners, his seventh spending plan in a row to do so.

The $1.6 billion plan would knock the tax rate down by 25 cents to an average of $5.42 per $1,000 assessed value. But Bello warned that the county is facing rising costs in several areas, combined with reduced or stagnant reimbursement rates from the state and federal government. His plan uses $33 million in reserve funds to offset those costs while holding spending growth below the rate of inflation.

"We continue to face growing financial pressure from unfunded federal and state mandates, and rising costs of pensions, healthcare and operating county government," Bello said in a release. “These growing obligations put increasing pressure on county taxpayers and are simply not sustainable over the long term.”

Much of the reserve funds are going to offset a $15 million hit the county took when the federal government changed certain reimbursement formulas for the SNAP food assistance program. For example, the county will receive half what it used to in reimbursed administrative costs, translating to a loss of $4.3 million, Bello said.

In other areas, reimbursement rates are not keeping up with expenses for services the county is required to provide by law. For example, Medicaid reimbursement rates have not kept pace with the increasing costs of providing care at Monroe Community Hospital.

And while New York requires its counties to provide Early Intervention and preschool special education services to children with developmental delays and disabilities, it has not adequately increased funding to do so, Bello said.

The budget includes $2 million toward a universal childcare trial program in Monroe County, which is getting $22 million from the state. Bello said that effort will add 1,000 childcare slots for Monroe County families with children up to 3 years old regardless of income.

And that cut to the tax rate — Bello said that was made possible by increasing property values in Monroe County and growth in the tax base.

local.body: A Cheektowaga man has been charged after allegedly communicating with a minor in a sexual manner.Bryce Weston, 22, was arrested and charged with criminal complaint with production of child sexual abuse material. Weston faces a minimum penalty of 15 years in prison, a maximum of 30 years and a fine of $250,000.According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, on August 23, Snapchat reported to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children that a file containing child pornography was uploaded to the server. The file was traced to Weston.According to the U.S. Attorney's Office, on October 14, the NYSP executed a search warrant at Weston's home on Columbus Avenue. Police recovered Weston's cell phone and found a chat conversation with a girl who identified herself as 13 years old. Weston allegedly identified himself as "Jake" and claimed he was "15 gonna be 16," with the communication quickly turning sexual in nature. The U.S. Attorney's Office said Weston continued to communicate with the minor, allegedly indicating he wanted to meet in person. Weston allegedly said in a conversation he was 20 years old, and the minor again stated she was 13 years old. Lauren Sánchez Bezos is heralding the start of après-ski season in style.

During her NYC press tour for her new children’s book “The Fly Who Flew to the North Pole” on Tuesday, the author leaned into the winter weather with her choice of novelty handbag.

Clad in a black Balenciaga sweater dress and knee-high boots, Sánchez Bezos toted Louis Vuitton’s LV Lodge bag , which is shaped like a miniature ski chalet and retails for $5,950.

“Comprising 65 different elements, this detailed design is made from cowhide leather with Monogram canvas trims and opens at the roof to store small daily items inside,” according to the purse’s product page.

Earlier in the day, Jeff Bezos’ wife donned a ’90s-era Thierry Mugler skirt suit in plush red velvet for an appearance on “Extra.”

She wore a second archival look — a black bodysuit styled with a vintage Chanel miniskirt in red tweed and black faux fur — for her “CBS Mornings” sit-down, accessorizing with a clutch inspired by her new book’s cover.

“To every kid who’s ever felt a step behind: you’re going places. Sometimes you just need a friend for the trip,” Sánchez Bezos wrote on Instagram .

We know Sánchez Bezos loves an après-ski fashion moment; she often spends the snowy months in Aspen, where she’s stepped out wearing everything from vintage Dior by John Galliano to Bottega Veneta and plush furs .

entertainment.title: Watch Brandy and Monica, Sheryl Crow & Maren Morris Perform Live for ‘Grammy Night’ on ‘DWTS’
entertainment.summary: The musicians soundtracked dance-offs between six of the competing pairs.
entertainment.body:
Dancing With the Stars welcomed a few extra stars to the stage on Tuesday (Nov. 10), with the show’s “Grammy Night” episode adding live music provided by Brandy and Monica , Sheryl Crow and Maren Morris to the program.

The special guests performed some of their most recognizable tracks as six pairs competed against each other side by side during dance-offs, each fighting for their ability to stay another week on the ballroom competition show. The two R&B icons stepped out to sing their staple 1998 13-week Billboard Hot 100 -topper, “The Boy Is Mine,” as Amber Glenn and Ezra Frech tried to out-rumba each other with routines happening simultaneously on stage, accompanied by their respective pros, Pasha Pashkov and Daniella Karagach.

Crow spent her time on stage playing 1994’s “All I Wanna Do,” strumming a glossy black guitar as Connor Wood and pro Rylee Arnold faced off against Maura Higgins and pro Mark Ballas, both couples showcasing their take on the cha cha. Jenna Dewan and pro Val Chmerkovskiy also cha cha’d, going toe to toe with Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik as Morris sang her 2018 smash “The Middle,” sans song partners Zedd and Grey.

Despite winning against Ali and Ravnik, Dewan and Chmerkovskiy ended up as the eliminated pair this week.

The episode marked DWTS ‘ first-ever “Grammy Night,” which featured artists and songs who’ve either won or been nominated at the Grammys . “The Middle” was nominated for record of the year and best pop duo/group performance in 2019, while “All I Wanna Do” took home record of the year and best female pop vocal in 1994. “The Boy Is Mine” won best R&B performance by a duo or group with vocal in 1999.

Five-time Grammy winner Janet Jackson also made a cameo on the Tuesday episode, appearing in a video message to Dewan, whose other performance on the show that night was to seven week 2001 Hot 100 No. 1 “All for You.”

“I am so excited,” Miss Jackson said in the clip. “I cannot wait to watch you perform tonight.”

entertainment.title: TV Ratings: ‘SNL’ Hits Two-Year High With Druski as Host
entertainment.summary: The Nov. 7 episode also had a big college football lead-in.
entertainment.body:
Logo text The Nov. 7 episode of Saturday Night Live scored its biggest same-day audience in two years with the hosting debut of comedian and online creator Druski. Having a big college football lead-in probably helped too.

SNL drew about 5.6 million viewers for the episode, which also featured musical guest the Strokes. It added about 440,000 viewers from the previous season high of 5.16 million a week earlier. The 5.6 million viewers is the best showing for SNL in almost exactly two years: The Nov. 2, 2024, edition delivered about 6.8 million viewers.
